questions.question: Which OSI layer handles logical addressing and routing?
questions.explanation: Layer 3 (Network) handles logical addressing (IP addresses) and routing between networks. Layer 2 handles MAC addressing within a network segment.

questions.question: What is the loopback address for IPv4?
questions.explanation: 127.0.0.1 (the 127.0.0.0/8 range) is the IPv4 loopback address used to test local TCP/IP stack. Pinging it tests the NIC driver without sending traffic on the network.

questions.question: What is the purpose of DNS?
options: Translate domain names to IP addresses
questions.explanation: DNS (Domain Name System) translates human-readable domain names (e.g., google.com) into IP addresses. It uses a hierarchical distributed database.

questions.question: Which wireless standard operates on both 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands?
questions.explanation: 802.11n (Wi-Fi 4) operates on both 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz. 802.11a and 802.11ac use 5 GHz only. 802.11b and 802.11g use 2.4 GHz only.

questions.question: What does VLAN stand for and what problem does it solve?
options: Virtual LAN — segments a physical network into multiple logical broadcast domains
Virtual Link — connects two remote offices
Very Large Area Network — describes large campus networks
Variable Length Address Network — supports CIDR notation
questions.explanation: VLANs logically segment a single physical switch into multiple broadcast domains, improving security, performance, and network management without requiring separate hardware.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a subnet mask?
options: Identifies which portion of an IP address is the network vs host
questions.explanation: A subnet mask defines the boundary between the network portion and host portion of an IP address. Devices in the same subnet can communicate directly; others require a router.

questions.question: Which protocol dynamically maps IP addresses to MAC addresses?
questions.explanation: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) dynamically maps a known IPv4 address to an unknown MAC address by broadcasting an ARP request on the local network.

questions.question: What is the function of NAT in networking?
options: Translates private IP addresses to public IPs for internet communication
questions.explanation: NAT (Network Address Translation) allows multiple devices with private IPs to share one or more public IPs, conserving IPv4 addresses and providing a layer of security.

questions.question: A network cable test shows a 'split pair' fault. What does this mean?
options: Two wires from different pairs are swapped, causing crosstalk
Both ends of the cable have the same pinout
questions.explanation: A split pair occurs when wires from different twisted pairs are connected together. It passes a continuity test but causes excessive crosstalk and poor performance.

questions.question: Which port does SMTP use by default?
questions.explanation: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) uses port 25 for server-to-server email relay. Port 587 is used for authenticated client-to-server submission. Port 110 is POP3, 143 is IMAP.

questions.question: What is the maximum cable length for Cat5e/Cat6 UTP in a standard Ethernet run?
questions.explanation: The maximum segment length for 10BASE-T, 100BASE-TX, and 1000BASE-T over UTP (Cat5e/Cat6) is 100 meters (328 feet), including patch cables.

questions.question: What type of attack involves flooding a network switch with random MAC addresses to overflow its CAM table?
questions.explanation: MAC flooding attacks overwhelm a switch's CAM (Content Addressable Memory) table. When full, the switch broadcasts all frames, allowing an attacker to capture traffic.

questions.question: Which routing protocol uses the Bellman-Ford algorithm?
questions.explanation: RIP (Routing Information Protocol) uses the Bellman-Ford algorithm and hop count as its metric. OSPF uses Dijkstra's SPF algorithm, EIGRP uses DUAL.

questions.question: What is a DMZ in network security?
options: A physical network segment between the internet and internal network that hosts public-facing services
The default VLAN on a switch
questions.explanation: A DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) is a network segment that sits between the internet and the internal LAN, hosting publicly accessible servers (web, mail) while protecting the internal network.

questions.question: What does the acronym QoS stand for, and what is its purpose?
options: Quality of Servers — managing server performance
Quality of Service — prioritizing network traffic to ensure performance for critical applications
Queue of Sessions — tracking active connections
Quantity of Subnets — number of network segments
questions.explanation: QoS (Quality of Service) mechanisms prioritize certain types of traffic (VoIP, video conferencing) over others (file downloads) to ensure acceptable performance for time-sensitive applications.

questions.question: Which IPv6 address starts with FE80::/10?
questions.explanation: Link-local addresses (FE80::/10) are automatically assigned to every IPv6 interface and are only valid on the local link. They are never routed beyond the local segment.

questions.question: What is the difference between a hub and a switch?
options: A hub sends frames to all ports; a switch uses MAC addresses to forward frames only to the destination port
A switch works at Layer 1; a hub at Layer 2
A hub is faster than a switch
questions.explanation: Hubs broadcast to all ports (Layer 1 — creates collision domain). Switches forward frames only to the destination port based on MAC address tables (Layer 2), reducing collisions.

questions.question: What protocol is used to securely manage network devices over an encrypted connection?
questions.explanation: SSH (Secure Shell) provides encrypted remote access for device management, replacing the insecure Telnet. SSH uses port 22 and provides authentication and encryption.

questions.question: A user can ping by IP but not by hostname. What is most likely the issue?
questions.explanation: If ping by IP works but hostname fails, name resolution is the issue. The DNS server may be unreachable, the wrong DNS server is configured, or the hostname doesn't exist in DNS.

questions.question: What is a Rogue DHCP server attack?
options: A DHCP server that assigns duplicate IPs
An unauthorized DHCP server that gives clients incorrect network settings (wrong gateway or DNS), enabling a man-in-the-middle attack
A DHCP server that has crashed
A server that exhausts the DHCP pool
questions.explanation: A rogue DHCP server responds to client requests before the legitimate server, providing a malicious default gateway (attacker's device) to intercept traffic — a man-in-the-middle attack.

questions.question: What is LLDP and how does it differ from CDP?
options: LLDP (Link Layer Discovery Protocol) is the IEEE 802.1AB vendor-neutral standard; CDP is Cisco-proprietary. Both discover directly connected devices
questions.explanation: LLDP (IEEE 802.1AB) is the open-standard equivalent of Cisco's CDP. Both advertise device capabilities, port info, and IP addresses at Layer 2. Most modern multi-vendor environments use LLDP.

questions.question: What is SNMP and what is it used for?
options: Simple Network Management Protocol — used to monitor and manage network devices by querying and setting device parameters
questions.explanation: SNMP (v1, v2c, v3) allows network management systems (NMS) to poll device stats (CPU, interfaces, errors) and configure devices. SNMPv3 adds encryption and authentication — always use v3 in production.

questions.question: What is a network baseline?
options: A documented record of normal network performance metrics used to identify deviations that may indicate problems
questions.explanation: A baseline captures normal performance (bandwidth utilization, latency, error rates, CPU). When issues arise, comparing current metrics against the baseline quickly identifies anomalies.

questions.question: Which protocol provides redundant default gateway capability in a vendor-neutral way?
questions.explanation: VRRP (Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol) is the IEEE standard for default gateway redundancy — vendor neutral. HSRP and GLBP are Cisco-proprietary. All use a virtual IP/MAC shared among routers.

questions.question: What is MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching)?
options: A high-performance routing technique that uses short path labels rather than IP addresses to forward packets across a network
questions.explanation: MPLS assigns short labels to packets at ingress. Core routers forward based on labels (not IP lookups) — much faster. Widely used by ISPs for VPNs, Traffic Engineering, and connecting enterprise sites.

questions.question: What is the difference between half-duplex and full-duplex Ethernet?
options: Half-duplex: send OR receive (not simultaneously), used with hubs. Full-duplex: simultaneous send and receive, used with switches. No collisions in full-duplex
questions.explanation: Modern switched Ethernet uses full-duplex — simultaneous TX/RX, no collisions, no CSMA/CD needed. Half-duplex shares the medium — only one device transmits at a time using CSMA/CD collision avoidance.

questions.question: What is flow control in networking?
options: A mechanism to prevent a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver — signals the sender to pause or reduce transmission rate
questions.explanation: Flow control prevents buffer overflow at the receiver. Ethernet uses PAUSE frames (802.3x) in full-duplex. TCP uses its sliding window mechanism for end-to-end flow control.

questions.question: What does MTU stand for, and what is the standard Ethernet MTU?
options: Maximum Transmission Unit — 1500 bytes is the standard Ethernet MTU. Jumbo frames extend to 9000 bytes
questions.explanation: MTU defines the largest data unit transmitted without fragmentation. Standard Ethernet MTU = 1500 bytes. Jumbo frames (9000 bytes) reduce overhead for large data transfers (storage, HPC). MTU mismatch causes packet drops.

questions.question: What is split horizon in distance-vector routing?
options: Splitting a network into two halves
A loop prevention technique: a router does not advertise a route back out the interface it was learned from
Dividing routing updates into smaller packets
questions.explanation: Split horizon prevents routing loops by not advertising routes back the direction they came from. Split horizon with poison reverse sends the route back with infinite metric (poison) instead.

questions.question: What port does RDP use?
questions.explanation: RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) uses TCP/UDP port 3389 for Windows remote desktop connections. Exposing RDP directly to the internet is a major security risk — use VPN or RDP Gateway instead.

questions.question: What is a proxy server?
options: A server that routes Layer 3 traffic
An intermediary server between clients and the internet — provides caching, content filtering, anonymization, and access control
questions.explanation: A proxy server handles requests on behalf of clients. Forward proxy: clients → proxy → internet (anonymization, filtering). Reverse proxy: internet → proxy → servers (load balancing, SSL termination).

questions.question: What is ICMP and what is it used for?
options: Internet Control Message Protocol — used for error reporting, diagnostics (ping uses echo request/reply, traceroute uses TTL exceeded messages)
questions.explanation: ICMP is used by devices to send error messages and operational info. Ping = ICMP Echo Request/Reply. Traceroute = sends packets with TTL=1,2,3... and collects ICMP Time Exceeded messages from each hop.

questions.question: What is BGP and where is it used?
options: An interior routing protocol for small networks
Border Gateway Protocol — the routing protocol of the internet, used between autonomous systems (ISPs, large enterprises) to exchange routing information
questions.explanation: BGP (EGP) manages routing between autonomous systems (AS numbers). It's used by ISPs to exchange routes on the internet and by enterprises with multiple ISP connections (multihoming). Path vector protocol.

questions.question: What is a trunk port's 'native VLAN'?
options: The VLAN that carries untagged traffic on a trunk link. Both ends must match to avoid mismatched VLAN communication
questions.explanation: The native VLAN on a trunk receives untagged frames. Default is VLAN 1 on Cisco. If the native VLAN differs on each end of a trunk, traffic can hop VLANs (native VLAN mismatch attack vector).

questions.question: What is 802.1X port-based authentication?
options: A network access control standard that requires devices/users to authenticate before being allowed on the network — uses RADIUS as the authentication server
questions.explanation: 802.1X (NAC) blocks all traffic on a port until the client authenticates via EAP (RADIUS). Used in enterprise wired and wireless networks to prevent unauthorized devices from accessing the network.

questions.question: What is a wildcard mask in ACLs?
options: The inverse of a subnet mask — 0 bits must match, 1 bits are ignored. Used in ACLs and OSPF to define which IP bits must match
A subnet mask with all bits flipped unnecessarily
questions.explanation: Wildcard masks are the inverse of subnet masks: 255.255.255.0 → wildcard 0.0.0.255. In 'access-list permit 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255', the last octet is ignored, matching 10.0.0.0-10.0.0.255.

questions.question: What is PoE (Power over Ethernet)?
options: Delivers electrical power along with data over standard Ethernet cabling to devices like IP phones, APs, and cameras — eliminating separate power adapters
questions.explanation: PoE (802.3af: 15.4W), PoE+ (802.3at: 30W), and PoE++ (802.3bt: 60-100W) power IP phones, wireless APs, IP cameras, and IoT devices through the network cable — no separate power outlet needed.

questions.question: What is DNS TTL?
options: The time a DNS server stays online
Time To Live — specifies how long (in seconds) a DNS record is cached by resolvers before re-querying the authoritative server
The number of DNS hops allowed
questions.explanation: DNS TTL controls caching duration. Low TTL (300s) = faster DNS changes propagate but more queries to your DNS server. High TTL (86400s = 24h) = efficient caching but slower change propagation.

questions.question: What is a CAM table overflow attack?
options: Floods a switch with thousands of fake source MAC addresses, filling the CAM table and forcing the switch to broadcast all frames (fail-open), allowing traffic interception
questions.explanation: When a switch's MAC table is full, it broadcasts frames out all ports (acts like a hub). An attacker runs macof or similar tool to flood the table, enabling passive interception of traffic.

questions.question: What is the difference between TCP and UDP?
options: TCP: connection-oriented, reliable, ordered delivery, flow control, error correction. UDP: connectionless, faster, no guaranteed delivery. Use TCP for HTTP/SSH; UDP for DNS/VoIP/video
They are equivalent for most purposes
questions.explanation: TCP: three-way handshake, acknowledgements, retransmission, flow control — reliable but overhead. UDP: no connection setup, no ACKs — low latency, used for real-time applications where some packet loss is acceptable.

questions.question: What is the function of a RADIUS server?
options: Provides centralized Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) for network access — used for wireless 802.1X, VPN, and dial-up authentication
questions.explanation: RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) centralizes AAA for network access. A RADIUS client (switch/AP) forwards credentials to the RADIUS server, which authenticates against a directory (AD/LDAP).

questions.question: What is the purpose of a screened subnet (DMZ)?
options: A network segment between two firewalls hosting public-facing servers — outer firewall filters internet traffic, inner firewall protects internal LAN
questions.explanation: A true DMZ uses two firewalls: an outer firewall between internet and DMZ, and an inner firewall between DMZ and internal LAN. Servers in DMZ (web, mail, DNS) are accessible from the internet but isolated from internal network.

questions.question: What is a site survey in wireless networking?
options: An assessment of a physical location to determine optimal AP placement, channel plan, coverage, and interference sources before deploying wireless
A speed test of wireless connections
questions.explanation: Wireless site surveys (passive: listen, active: connect, predictive: software model) determine AP placement, channel assignments, power levels, and identify interference sources (microwaves, adjacent networks) before deployment.

questions.question: What is CSMA/CD?
options: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection — the mechanism used by classic Ethernet to detect and recover from collisions on shared media
questions.explanation: CSMA/CD: Listen before transmitting (carrier sense). If collision detected, jam, then wait random backoff time. Only relevant for half-duplex Ethernet (hubs). Full-duplex switched networks don't use CSMA/CD.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a network topology diagram?
options: Documents how network devices are physically or logically connected — essential for troubleshooting, planning, and change management
questions.explanation: Physical topology: actual cable/device layout. Logical topology: how data flows. Network diagrams help technicians understand the network, troubleshoot faster, and plan changes without disruption.

questions.question: What is the difference between a router and a Layer 3 switch?
options: They are identical in all ways

Both perform Layer 3 routing, but Layer 3 switches use hardware ASICs for wire-speed routing between VLANs. Routers handle more complex routing features (BGP, NAT, WAN protocols), LAN and WAN connectivity
L3 switches are for WAN only
questions.explanation: L3 switches route between VLANs at near-wire speed using hardware — ideal for inter-VLAN routing in the LAN. Routers excel at WAN connectivity, complex routing policies, NAT, and VPN — features typically not on L3 switches.

questions.question: What is 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6) and what are its key improvements?
options: Wi-Fi 6 operates on 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz with OFDMA, MU-MIMO (8x8), BSS Coloring, TWT — designed for high-density environments with up to 9.6 Gbps theoretical throughput
questions.explanation: Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) improvements: OFDMA (divide channels for multiple users simultaneously), MU-MIMO 8x8, BSS Coloring (reduces interference), TWT (Target Wake Time for IoT battery life). Wi-Fi 6E adds 6 GHz band.

questions.question: What is a network IDS signature?
options: A pattern or rule that matches known attack traffic — when network traffic matches a signature, the IDS generates an alert
questions.explanation: IDS/IPS signatures are patterns matching known attack traffic (e.g., SQL injection string in HTTP, specific exploit payload). Signature-based detection is effective for known attacks but misses zero-days (needs anomaly detection).

questions.question: What is the purpose of NTP (Network Time Protocol)?
options: Synchronizes clocks across network devices to a common time source — critical for log correlation, certificate validity, Kerberos authentication
questions.explanation: NTP synchronizes device clocks to UTC. Critical for: log correlation (events must be in correct time sequence), Kerberos authentication (5-minute skew tolerance), certificate validation, and scheduled operations.

questions.question: What is a VLAN hopping attack?
options: An attack exploiting DTP or native VLAN misconfigs to send traffic to a VLAN that shouldn't be accessible — allows accessing segmented network traffic
A method to extend VLANs over WAN
questions.explanation: VLAN hopping: (1) Switch spoofing — attacker's device negotiates a trunk with DTP; (2) Double tagging — attacker sends double-tagged frames to hop to native VLAN. Mitigation: disable DTP, change native VLAN from 1.

questions.question: What is a fiber optic cable and what are its advantages over copper?
options: Uses light pulses through glass/plastic fiber — immune to EMI, much greater bandwidth (100Gbps+), longer distances (up to 80km single-mode), no electrical hazards
questions.explanation: Fiber optic advantages: immune to electromagnetic interference, no ground loops, much longer distances (SMF: up to 80km, MMF: up to 2km), higher bandwidth (100G+ easier than copper), and secure (no signal radiation).

questions.question: What is the difference between single-mode and multi-mode fiber?
options: Single-mode (SMF): single light ray, longer distance (km), laser source, yellow jacket. Multi-mode (MMF): multiple light paths, shorter distance (up to 2km), LED/VCSEL source, orange/aqua jacket
questions.explanation: SMF: 8-10 micron core, single light path, longer distances, used for WAN/MAN. MMF: 50-62.5 micron core, multiple light paths (modal dispersion limits distance), used for campus/data center LAN (OM1-OM5).

questions.question: What is a DHCP lease and what happens when it expires?
options: A temporary IP address assignment with an expiry time. Client attempts renewal at 50% of lease time, then rebinds at 87.5%, then gets new IP from any DHCP server if still expired
questions.explanation: DHCP leases are temporary. At 50% expiry, client sends unicast renewal to original server. At 87.5%, broadcasts rebind request to any server. If no response, IP expires and client starts DORA process again.

questions.question: What is the OSI Physical layer responsible for?
options: Transmission of raw bits over a physical medium — defines electrical signals, cable types, connectors, and bit rates. No addressing at this layer
questions.explanation: Layer 1 (Physical) deals with: bit encoding, voltage levels, cable specs (Cat6, fiber), connectors (RJ45, LC, SC), transmission rates, and synchronization. Devices: hubs, repeaters, cabling. No addressing.

questions.question: What is the purpose of IPAM in network management?
options: IP Address Management — a tool/process for planning, tracking, and managing IP address space, DHCP servers, and DNS records centrally
questions.explanation: IPAM tools (Windows Server IPAM, phpIPAM, Infoblox) provide visibility into IP address utilization, prevent conflicts, manage DHCP scopes, and integrate with DNS. Critical for large networks to avoid IP chaos.

questions.question: What is the default subnet mask for a Class B network?
questions.explanation: Class B (128.0.0.0–191.255.255.255) has a default mask of 255.255.0.0 (/16), providing 16 bits for hosts (65,534 usable). Class A = 255.0.0.0 (/8), Class C = 255.255.255.0 (/24).

questions.question: What is a network loop and how does STP prevent it?
options: A routing loop between two ISPs
A Layer 2 loop where frames circulate indefinitely, causing broadcast storms and switch MAC table instability. STP prevents this by blocking redundant paths (ports in blocking state)
questions.explanation: Layer 2 loops: frames have no TTL (unlike IP), so looping frames multiply exponentially causing broadcast storms. STP (802.1D) selects a root bridge and blocks redundant paths, creating a loop-free tree topology.

questions.question: What is an out-of-band management network?
options: A dedicated separate management network used to access and manage network devices even when the production network is down — uses console servers, dedicated management interfaces
questions.explanation: OOB management uses separate physical connectivity (dedicated management ports, cellular modems, console servers). Critical for restoring failed devices when production network is unavailable.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a network access control (NAC) system?
options: Verifies that devices meet security policies (OS patch level, antivirus status, domain membership) before granting network access — non-compliant devices go to remediation VLAN
questions.explanation: NAC (Cisco ISE, Aruba ClearPass, Forescout) enforces posture assessment before allowing devices on the network. Can place non-compliant or unknown devices in quarantine VLANs for remediation.

questions.question: What ports does FTP use and why is it considered insecure?
options: Port 21 (control) and 20 (data — active mode). FTP transmits credentials and data in cleartext — easily intercepted. Use SFTP (SSH, port 22) or FTPS (TLS) instead
questions.explanation: FTP: port 21 for commands, port 20 for data (active mode) or ephemeral port (passive mode). All data including passwords transmitted in plaintext — never use over untrusted networks. SFTP (over SSH) or FTPS are secure alternatives.

questions.question: What is a VLAN hopping attack?
options: Exploiting trunk port misconfigurations (double-tagging or switch spoofing) to send traffic to a VLAN the attacker shouldn't access
questions.explanation: Double-tagging: attacker tags frame with two VLAN IDs; outer tag matches native VLAN (stripped by switch), inner tag reaches target VLAN. Prevention: set native VLAN to unused VLAN, enable VLAN pruning, use trunk access mode.

questions.question: What port does LDAP use?
questions.explanation: LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) uses TCP/UDP 389. LDAPS (LDAP over TLS) uses TCP 636. Used for directory queries (Active Directory, OpenLDAP). Always use LDAPS or LDAP with STARTTLS in production.

questions.question: What is a MAC flooding attack countermeasure?
options: Enable port security — limits the number of MAC addresses per switch port and shuts down the port (err-disabled) if the limit is exceeded
questions.explanation: Port security: 'switchport port-security maximum 2' limits MACs per port. Violation actions: Shutdown (err-disabled), Restrict (drop+log), Protect (drop). Prevents MAC table overflow/CAM flooding attacks.

questions.question: What is RADIUS and how does it differ from TACACS+?
options: RADIUS: open standard, encrypts only password, combines authentication+authorization. TACACS+: Cisco-proprietary, encrypts entire payload, separates authentication/authorization/accounting (AAA)
questions.explanation: Both are AAA protocols. RADIUS (UDP 1812/1813): open standard, widely supported, used for 802.1X/VPN. TACACS+ (TCP 49): Cisco-proprietary, encrypts full body, better for granular device administration.

questions.question: What does 'link-local' address range mean in networking?
options: Addresses only valid on a directly-connected segment — not routed. IPv4: 169.254.0.0/16 (APIPA). IPv6: fe80::/10 (mandatory on every interface). Used for neighbor discovery and ARP
questions.explanation: Link-local addresses are limited to the local link — no router will forward them. IPv4 APIPA 169.254.x.x appears when DHCP fails. IPv6 link-local (fe80::) is automatically configured on every interface and used for NDP.

questions.question: What is VLAN trunking using 802.1Q vs ISL?
options: 802.1Q (IEEE standard): inserts a 4-byte tag into the Ethernet frame, supports native VLAN. ISL (Cisco-proprietary): encapsulates the entire frame in a new header — obsolete, replaced by 802.1Q
questions.explanation: 802.1Q is the universal standard: adds a 4-byte tag between source MAC and EtherType fields. ISL is legacy Cisco-only and encapsulates the entire original frame — no longer used in modern networks.

questions.question: What is the difference between RJ-45 and RJ-11?
options: RJ-45: 8P8C connector for Ethernet networking (Cat5e/Cat6). RJ-11: 6P2C connector for telephone lines — smaller than RJ-45
questions.explanation: RJ-45 has 8 positions/8 contacts, used for Ethernet (Cat5e, Cat6, Cat6a). RJ-11 has 6 positions/2-4 contacts, used for analog phone and DSL. RJ-45 connectors are too wide to fit RJ-11 ports.

questions.question: What is Cat6 vs Cat6a cable?
options: Cat6: 1 Gbps up to 55m for 10GbE (100m for 1GbE). Cat6a: 10 Gbps up to 100m for 10GbE — augmented specification with better alien crosstalk protection and thicker cables
questions.explanation: Cat6: 250 MHz bandwidth, 1 GbE @ 100m, 10 GbE @ 55m. Cat6a: 500 MHz, 10 GbE @ 100m. Cat6a cables are heavier, harder to bend. Use Cat6a for data centers or anywhere 10GbE is needed over full runs.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a patch panel?
options: A passive panel in a rack that terminates horizontal cable runs from wall jacks — allows flexible port-to-switch connections via patch cords without disturbing permanent cabling
questions.explanation: Patch panels terminate structured cabling (permanent runs from wall plates). Short patch cords connect panel ports to switch ports. Changing connections is easy (move a patch cord) without touching in-wall cabling.

questions.question: What is an OTDR used for in fiber optics?
options: Optical Time Domain Reflectometer — sends a pulse into fiber and measures reflections to pinpoint the location and severity of breaks, splices, connectors, and bends
questions.explanation: OTDR maps a fiber run graphically, showing loss events and their distances. Essential for: locating breaks, verifying splice quality, commissioning new runs. Much more powerful than a simple light source and power meter.

questions.question: What is a half-open (SYN) scan in network reconnaissance?
options: Sends SYN packets to discover open ports — if SYN-ACK received (port open), sends RST instead of completing handshake. Stealthier than full connect scan as no full connection is logged
questions.explanation: SYN (half-open) scan: attacker sends SYN → if SYN-ACK comes back, port is open → attacker sends RST to abort. Faster than full connect scan and leaves fewer log entries. Used by Nmap (-sS flag).

questions.question: What is network address translation and what problem does it solve?
options: Maps private RFC1918 addresses to public IP addresses for internet communication — extends IPv4 address space by allowing many devices to share one public IP
questions.explanation: NAT (and specifically PAT) allows private IPs (10.x, 172.16-31.x, 192.168.x) to share a single public IP using port multiplexing. Solved IPv4 exhaustion. Also provides a level of security by hiding internal topology.

questions.question: What is NetFlow/sFlow used for?
options: Records network flow statistics (source/destination IP, ports, protocol, byte/packet counts) for traffic analysis, bandwidth monitoring, and anomaly detection
questions.explanation: NetFlow (Cisco) and IPFIX (IETF standard) collect metadata about network conversations. Exported to a collector for analysis. Use cases: top talkers, bandwidth accounting, security anomaly detection, capacity planning.

questions.question: What is an anycast address?
options: One IP address assigned to multiple nodes — traffic is routed to the topologically nearest node (routing protocol determines this). Used by DNS root servers and CDNs
questions.explanation: Anycast assigns the same IP to multiple servers in different locations. Packets are routed to the nearest server by BGP shortest path. Used by DNS (root servers use anycast), CDNs, and DoH/DoT services.

questions.question: What is the difference between fiber SMF and MMF?
options: SMF (Single-Mode Fiber): tiny core (~9µm), laser source, up to 100km+ for long-haul. MMF (Multi-Mode Fiber): larger core (50/62.5µm), LED/VCSEL source, up to 550m — cheaper, used in buildings/data centers
questions.explanation: SMF: one light path, no modal dispersion, very long distances (telecom, inter-building). MMF: multiple light paths (modal dispersion limits distance), cheaper optics, used for shorter runs within buildings and data centers.

questions.question: What is a rogue access point?
options: An authorized AP with wrong settings
An unauthorized wireless AP connected to a wired network — allows attackers to bypass perimeter security by creating a wireless entry point. Detected via wireless surveys and NAC
An AP in a public place
questions.explanation: Rogue APs: attacker plugs an AP into a corporate switch or an employee sets up a personal hotspot. Creates unauthorized entry point. Detection: wireless surveys, 802.1X NAC, rogue detection in WLC/WDS systems.

questions.question: What is a Wireshark capture filter vs display filter?
options: Capture filter: written in BPF syntax, limits what packets are captured (reduces file size). Display filter: written in Wireshark filter language, filters already-captured packets for analysis
questions.explanation: Capture filter (BPF): 'tcp port 443' — only captures HTTPS. Better for performance on busy networks. Display filter: 'http.request.method == GET' — flexible post-capture analysis. Apply both for efficient captures.

questions.question: What is the OSI Layer responsible for end-to-end delivery and reliability?
options: Layer 4 — Transport (TCP provides reliable ordered delivery; UDP provides fast unreliable delivery). This layer provides: segmentation, flow control, error correction, and port numbers
questions.explanation: Layer 4 (Transport): TCP — connection-oriented, reliable, ordered, flow-controlled. UDP — connectionless, fast, no guarantee. Port numbers at Layer 4 identify services (HTTP=80, SSH=22, HTTPS=443).

questions.question: What is IPAM (IP Address Management)?
options: A system for planning, tracking, and managing IP address space allocation across a network — integrates with DNS and DHCP for unified DDI management
questions.explanation: IPAM tools (Microsoft IPAM, ManageEngine, InfoBlox) track what IPs are allocated, available, and to which devices. DDI (DNS-DHCP-IPAM) integrates all three for automated IP lifecycle management in large networks.

questions.question: What is a network baseline and why is it important?
options: A documented record of normal performance metrics (bandwidth, latency, CPU, errors) used to detect anomalies and troubleshoot by comparing current state to normal state
questions.explanation: Without a baseline, you can't tell what 'normal' looks like. When users report 'the network is slow,' compare current metrics to baseline. Helps distinguish between actual outage, normal load, and misuse.

questions.question: What is GRE tunnel keepalive?
options: Periodically sends keepalive messages through the GRE tunnel to verify the remote end is reachable — allows routing protocols to detect tunnel failure and reroute traffic
questions.explanation: GRE keepalives detect when the remote tunnel endpoint is unreachable (even if the physical interface is up). Without keepalives, the tunnel interface stays up and routing protocols don't detect the failure. Configured with 'tunnel keepalive'.

questions.question: What is the 568A vs 568B wiring standard?
options: 568A and 568B are TIA/EIA wiring standards for RJ-45 connectors — they use different pin pair arrangements. A straight-through cable uses same standard on both ends; a crossover uses 568A on one end and 568B on the other
questions.explanation: Both 568A and 568B are valid. Organizations standardize on one (most use 568B). Straight-through: same standard both ends — connects PC to switch. Crossover: 568A one end, 568B the other — connects PC to PC or switch to switch (modern NICs auto-MDIX makes crossovers unnecessary).

questions.question: What does DHCP lease time control?
options: How long a client holds a DHCP-assigned IP before renewal. Shorter: IP pool refreshes faster, good for guest networks. Longer: reduces DHCP traffic, better for stable devices
How secure the DHCP process is
questions.explanation: Short lease (1-2 hours): for guest/public Wi-Fi where devices come and go. Long lease (8 days): for corporate servers with stable IPs. Too-short leases cause excessive DHCP traffic; too-long can exhaust pools.

questions.question: What is a syslog server and what are syslog severity levels?
options: A centralized server receiving log messages from network devices. Severity 0-7: Emergency (0), Alert (1), Critical (2), Error (3), Warning (4), Notice (5), Informational (6), Debug (7)
questions.explanation: Syslog (UDP 514, TCP 6514 for TLS) forwards device logs to a central server. Common mnemonic: Every Awful Crisis Eventually Will Neglect Innocent Demons. Level 3 and above warrant immediate investigation.

questions.question: What is a broadcast storm and what causes it?
options: A network loop causes frames to circulate endlessly, multiplying exponentially until bandwidth is saturated and devices crash. Caused by: missing STP, cabling loops, STP failure
questions.explanation: Broadcast storms occur when Ethernet frames loop between switches. Without STP, a single loop causes exponential frame multiplication. Symptoms: 100% link utilization, switch CPU at max, network unresponsive. STP prevents this.

questions.question: What is the difference between half-duplex and full-duplex collisions?
options: Half-duplex: CSMA/CD detects and retransmits after collisions. Full-duplex: no collisions possible (separate TX/RX pairs) — CSMA/CD disabled. Modern switched Ethernet is always full-duplex
questions.explanation: In half-duplex (hubs), only one device sends at a time; collisions trigger backoff/retransmit. In full-duplex (switches), dedicated TX/RX pairs prevent collisions entirely — CSMA/CD is disabled for better performance.

questions.question: What is a supernet or CIDR block aggregation?
options: Combining multiple contiguous network blocks into a single larger prefix for routing table efficiency. E.g., 192.168.0.0/24 + 192.168.1.0/24 → 192.168.0.0/23
questions.explanation: Supernetting (route aggregation) advertises multiple contiguous networks as one summary route — reduces routing table size on internet-facing routers. ISPs aggregate customer prefixes; enterprises aggregate branch routes.

questions.question: What is TTL in DNS vs TTL in IP packets?
options: DNS TTL: how long (seconds) a resolver caches a DNS record before re-querying the authoritative server. IP TTL: hop count — decremented by each router, drops packet at 0 to prevent routing loops
DNS TTL is measured in hops
questions.explanation: DNS TTL controls cache duration (low=fast propagation, high=efficient). IP TTL (IPv4)/Hop Limit (IPv6) prevents infinite routing loops — each router decrements by 1. Different concepts that happen to share a name.

questions.question: What is the purpose of IEEE 802.3af/at/bt standards?
options: Power over Ethernet (PoE) standards: 802.3af (PoE): 15.4W, 802.3at (PoE+): 30W, 802.3bt (PoE++): 60W/100W — power IP phones, APs, cameras, and IoT devices over Cat5e/6 cable
questions.explanation: PoE standards deliver power and data over Ethernet. 802.3af: basic PoE for IP phones, small APs. 802.3at: PoE+ for PTZ cameras, tablets. 802.3bt: PoE++ for laptops, multi-radio APs, smart lighting systems.

questions.question: What is a network diagram and what are the key types?
options: Logical diagram: shows IP addressing, VLANs, routing — not physical layout. Physical diagram: shows actual device locations, cable runs, rack positions. Essential for planning, troubleshooting, and documentation
Diagrams are optional for small networks
questions.explanation: Good network documentation includes: logical diagrams (Layer 2/3 topology, IP schemes, VLAN maps), physical diagrams (where devices are, cable paths), and rack diagrams. Without documentation, troubleshooting takes much longer.

questions.question: What is nmap and what are common scan types?
options: An open-source network scanner for host discovery and service enumeration. Common scans: -sn (ping sweep), -sS (SYN scan), -sV (version detection), -sU (UDP), -A (aggressive: OS+version+scripts)
questions.explanation: Nmap is the standard network reconnaissance tool. Common uses: discover live hosts, enumerate open ports, detect service versions, identify OS. Use with permission only — unauthorized scanning is illegal in many jurisdictions.

questions.question: What is jumbo frames and when should they be used?
options: Ethernet frames larger than the standard 1500 byte MTU — typically 9000 bytes for jumbo frames. Benefits: reduced CPU overhead for large transfers. Use cases: storage (iSCSI, NFS), VM migration, HPC — requires network-wide support
questions.explanation: Jumbo frames require all devices in the path to support the larger MTU — switch, NIC, and any intermediate devices. If one device doesn't support jumbo frames, traffic drops (MTU mismatch). Enable per-interface, ensure end-to-end consistency.

questions.question: What is the purpose of OSPF Hello interval and Dead interval?
options: Hello: frequency of keepalive packets (default 10s on broadcast, 30s on NBMA). Dead: how long to wait before declaring neighbor down (default 4x Hello). Both must match on adjacent routers for adjacency to form
questions.explanation: OSPF Hello and Dead intervals must match between neighbors. Default: Hello=10s, Dead=40s on Ethernet. Mismatch = no adjacency. Lower timers = faster failure detection but more CPU/bandwidth. Never-match is a common misconfiguration.

questions.question: What is 802.1Q in Q (QinQ / VLAN stacking)?
options: 802.1ad (QinQ / Provider Bridging): allows adding an outer VLAN tag to frames already tagged with an inner VLAN — enables SPs to tunnel customer VLANs across provider networks while using their own VLAN space
questions.explanation: QinQ encapsulates customer 802.1Q frames inside a provider S-Tag (outer VLAN). Customer can use any VLAN IDs (1-4094) — the provider only sees the outer S-Tag. Common in metro Ethernet and ISP aggregation networks.

questions.question: What is a default route and how does it affect routing decisions?
options: A route for 0.0.0.0/0 — matches any destination not found in the routing table. The 'gateway of last resort'. All unmatched packets follow this route (typically toward an ISP or firewall)
questions.explanation: The default route (0.0.0.0/0) is the least specific route — matches everything. Routers apply longest prefix match: /32 > /24 > /16 > /0. The default route catches all traffic with no more-specific match and forwards it upstream.

questions.question: What is a network convergence time?
options: Time to set up a new network
The time required for all routers in a network to update their routing tables and agree on the network topology after a change (link up/down, route change). Faster protocols = lower convergence time
questions.explanation: Convergence: OSPF typically converges in seconds (SPF delay); EIGRP can converge in milliseconds (DUAL with feasible successors). BGP is slow (minutes for full internet convergence). During convergence, packets may be dropped or loop.

questions.question: What is the difference between an IDS and a honeypot in network security?
options: IDS: passively monitors traffic/logs for known attack patterns and alerts — reactive. Honeypot: a decoy system designed to attract attackers and observe their techniques — proactive intelligence gathering
questions.explanation: IDS (Intrusion Detection System): monitors real production traffic for attacks. Honeypot: fake vulnerable system to lure attackers away from real assets and study their methods. Both are complementary security controls.

questions.question: What is NTP stratum?
options: Indicates clock source accuracy distance. Stratum 0: atomic/GPS clock. Stratum 1: directly synced to Stratum 0. Stratum 2: synced from Stratum 1. Maximum useful stratum is 15 — 16 means unsynchronized
questions.explanation: NTP stratum measures distance from reference clock. Always sync critical servers to Stratum 1 or 2 servers. Stratum 1 = gold standard (GPS/atomic). Each hop adds potential drift. NTP v4 uses UDP 123.

questions.question: What is 'split DNS' (split-horizon DNS)?
options: Serving different DNS records to internal vs external queries for the same domain — internal users get private IPs, external users get public IPs. Reduces attack surface and improves security
questions.explanation: Split DNS runs separate zone files for internal/external. 'corp.example.com' resolves to 10.1.1.100 internally (direct access) vs 203.0.113.5 externally (through load balancer/WAF). Hides internal IP schema from internet.

questions.question: What is port mirroring (SPAN)?
options: Copies traffic from one or more switch ports or VLANs to a designated monitor port where a packet analyzer or IDS can inspect it — non-disruptive traffic capture
questions.explanation: SPAN (Switched Port Analyzer) mirrors traffic to an analysis port. Local SPAN: same switch. RSPAN: across switches via a RSPAN VLAN. ERSPAN: over GRE tunnel to a remote analyzer. Used for IDS, packet capture, performance monitoring.
